chapters.title: Mijbil the Otter
chapters.summary: Gavin Maxwell, mourning his dead dog Jonnie, is advised by a friend to keep an otter at Camusfearna, his water-ringed home in Scotland. From the Tigris marshes of Iraq he gets a young otter he names Mijbil, whose love of water and mischievous games fill the house with life. The chapter follows their eventful flight to England and the comic confusion Mijbil causes on the streets of London.
hotTopics: Mijbil's arrival from the Tigris marshes and his naming
Mijbil and the bathroom tap: his love of water
The air journey: the box, the torn lining and the escape in the plane
The kind air hostess and the two bowls of water
Mijbil in the streets of London: the wild guesses and the labourer's answer
Theme: the bond between man and animal

sections.heading: Plot Summary
points: After his pet dog Jonnie dies, Gavin Maxwell feels an emptiness at Camusfearna, his home in the Scottish Highlands; a friend suggests an otter, since the house ringed by water is just right for a water-loving pet.
While Maxwell is in Basra in southern Iraq, two Arabs bring him a young otter from the Tigris marshes, and he names it Mijbil.
Mijbil is at first aloof and indifferent, but soon grows affectionate and shows a passion for water, fumbling with the tap and playing in the bathtub.
He invents his own games, including playing with small rubber balls, and fills the flat with his galloping energy.

To take Mij to England, Maxwell books a flight to Paris on another airline since the regular airline will not carry animals; Mij must travel in a box of not more than two feet square, tears its lining and escapes in the aircraft, where a kind air hostess helps.
In London, passers-by guess wildly that Mij is a baby seal, squirrel, walrus, hippo or even a brontosaurus; only a labourer, without looking up, correctly calls him an otter.

keyTerms.meaning: Maxwell's home in the Scottish Highlands, ringed by water
wetlands in Iraq from where the otter was brought
the name Maxwell gave his otter, later shortened to Mij
the name zoologists gave to Mijbil's previously unknown race
Maxwell's pet dog whose death left him lonely
a town in southern Iraq where Maxwell stayed

sections.trick: Recall the journey in four beats: tap, box, plane, labourer; the story moves from bathroom games to a flight adventure to street comedy.
sections.examPointer: Fact questions usually target the reason for choosing an otter, the box rule of two feet square and the London guesses; keep Gavin Maxwell's name and the Iraq connection exact.

sections.heading: Themes and Message
points: Companionship heals loss; the otter fills the empty place left by Maxwell's dead dog.
Curiosity and play are natural to animals, as Mij invents games and explores the tap on his own.
Caring for a wild pet demands patience, planning and adjustment, as the air journey shows.
Strangers can show unexpected kindness, like the air hostess who understands Mij's love of water.
Gentle humour runs through the chapter, from the soaked bathroom to the wild guesses in London.
Message: animals feel, play and bond with humans, so they deserve empathy and thoughtful care.

keyTerms.meaning: the pleasant feeling of having someone to share life with
the ability to understand and share the feelings of another
eager to know and explore things
a light, fun-loving quality full of games
calm endurance without complaint

sections.trick: Theme formula: Loss, Love, Labour, Laughter; loneliness cured by love, effort taken for the journey, and comic incidents throughout.
sections.examPointer: When asked for the theme, support it with two incidents, the tap game and the flight chaos, instead of writing general statements.

sections.heading: Character Sketch
points: Mijbil is playful and curious; he fumbles with the tap, soaks himself and spends long stretches playing in water.
He is intelligent and inventive, making games out of small rubber balls and turning everyday objects into toys.
He is affectionate once he trusts, staying close to Maxwell and settling happily into home life.
He is restless and adventurous during travel, tearing the box lining and slipping out to run along the aircraft aisle.
Maxwell is a patient, observant owner who watches Mij like a naturalist and adjusts all his plans for the pet's comfort.
Maxwell is determined and resourceful, arranging a special box and a difficult route just to carry Mij safely to England.

keyTerms.meaning: full of fun and games
distant and reserved, showing no warmth
a person who studies animals and plants scientifically
naughtily playful
showing love and fondness

sections.trick: Mij equals mischief plus love of water; Maxwell equals the patient planner; pair every trait with one incident.
sections.examPointer: Character answers earn marks when traits are proved by incidents; quote the plane escape or the tap game as evidence.

sections.heading: Important Word Meanings
points: Learn meanings in context; for example, aloof describes Mij's cold behaviour in his first days.
Use these words while writing answers to show a good vocabulary range.
Practise the spellings of unusual words like brontosaurus.
Make your own sentence with each word for quick revision.
Vocabulary questions are often picked from exactly such chapter words.

sections.trick: Link each word to its scene: aloof with the first days, fumble with the tap, drenched with the bathroom, lead with London walks, brontosaurus with the street guesses.
sections.examPointer: Even when no direct meaning question comes, correct word use in paragraph answers impresses the examiner.

sections.heading: Exam Focus
points: Remember why the friend suggested an otter and what kind of home Camusfearna was.
Learn the air journey details: the box of two feet square, the torn lining, the escape in the plane and the two bowls of water.
Recall the wrong guesses in London and the one correct answer given by the labourer.
Be ready to describe Mij's games with the tap and the rubber balls.
Value-based questions may ask about responsibility and kindness towards pets.

keyTerms.meaning: a question built around a quoted passage from the text
a conclusion drawn from clues in the text
a quality that defines a character's nature
the central idea of a chapter
a moral lesson that can be quoted in answers

sections.trick: Flight mnemonic: Rule, Rip, Run, Relief; the box rule, the torn lining, the run down the aisle and the kind hostess.
sections.examPointer: In extract-based MCQs, first identify the situation hidden in the lines; options often borrow words from other episodes to confuse you.

mcqs.question: Who is the author of the chapter 'Mijbil the Otter'?
mcqs.explanation: Gavin Maxwell, a Scottish writer and nature lover, wrote this chapter about his pet otter.

mcqs.question: After his dog Jonnie died, which pet did Maxwell's friend suggest?
mcqs.explanation: The friend advised an otter because Camusfearna, ringed by water, would suit a water-loving animal.

mcqs.question: What name did Maxwell give to the otter?
mcqs.explanation: He called the otter Mijbil, a name soon shortened to Mij.

mcqs.question: From where did Maxwell get the otter?
mcqs.explanation: While he was in southern Iraq, two Arabs brought him a young otter from the Tigris marshes.

mcqs.question: Why was Camusfearna considered a suitable home for an otter?
options: It was warm throughout the year
It had a large garden full of fish
It was close to a market
mcqs.explanation: The house stood close to the water, so an otter would feel perfectly at home there.

mcqs.question: "Mijbil, as I called the otter, was, in fact, of a race previously unknown to science." What distinction did Mijbil's race later receive?
options: It was declared the commonest otter of England
It was named after the author and called Maxwell's otter
It was banned as a dangerous species
It was declared a family of seals
mcqs.explanation: The race was new to science, and zoologists named it after Maxwell himself.

mcqs.question: "She brought two bowls of water, one for Mij to drink and one for him to play in." Who does 'she' refer to, and what does the gesture show?
options: A fellow passenger; her fear of animals
The pilot; his strictness about rules
The air hostess; her kindness and understanding of Mij's nature
The ticket collector; her sense of duty
mcqs.explanation: The charming air hostess co-operated warmly and thoughtfully gave the water-loving otter a bowl to play in.

mcqs.question: How did Mijbil amuse himself inside the author's house?
options: By chasing cats in the street
By digging holes in the garden
By playing with the tap in the bathtub and with small rubber balls
mcqs.explanation: Mij loved to jiggle the tap, play in water and invent games with small rubber balls.

mcqs.question: "The airline insisted that Mij should be packed into a box of not more than two feet square." What happened when Mij was left in this box before the flight?
options: He slept peacefully for an hour
He tore the lining apart and hurt himself, ending up covered in blood
He refused to enter the box at all
The box was lost at the airport
mcqs.explanation: Panicking inside the box, Mij ripped its lining apart and injured himself before the journey began.

mcqs.question: In the streets of London, who was the only person to identify Mij correctly?
options: A woman with a Pekinese dog
A schoolboy carrying a nature book
A labourer, who said 'otter' without even looking up
mcqs.explanation: Londoners guessed seal, squirrel, walrus, hippo and brontosaurus, but a working labourer casually gave the right answer.

boardQuestions.question: Why did Maxwell's friend suggest that he should keep an otter as a pet?
boardQuestions.answer: Maxwell's pet dog Jonnie had died, leaving him lonely at Camusfearna. His friend advised him to get an otter instead of another dog, because the house stood ringed by water, close to its edges, and such a setting would be ideal for a water-loving creature like an otter. Acting on this advice, Maxwell later received Mijbil in Iraq.

boardQuestions.question: How did Mijbil develop a love for water in the author's house?
boardQuestions.answer: Soon after arriving, Mijbil discovered the bathroom and developed a passion for water. He fumbled with the taps, learned to turn them on with his paws and played in the bathtub for long stretches, splashing water everywhere. What began as an accident became his favourite game, revealing an otter's instinctive delight in water.

boardQuestions.question: What difficulties did Maxwell face while flying Mijbil to England, and how were they overcome?
boardQuestions.answer: The regular airline refused to carry animals, so Maxwell booked a flight to Paris on another airline. Mij had to be packed in a box of not more than two feet square; he tore its lining and hurt himself. In the aircraft he escaped and ran along the aisle, alarming passengers, until the kind air hostess helped, later giving him two bowls of water, one to drink and one to play in.

boardQuestions.question: How did the people of London react to Mijbil when he was taken out for walks?
boardQuestions.answer: Londoners could not recognise an otter and reacted with comic curiosity. Passers-by stopped to stare and offered wild guesses, calling Mij a baby seal, a squirrel, a walrus, a hippo and even a brontosaurus. Almost everyone was wrong; the only person to name him correctly was a labourer who, without looking up from his work, simply said 'otter'. The episode shows how little city people know of wild animals.

boardQuestions.question: Draw a character sketch of Mijbil, the otter, with examples from the chapter.
boardQuestions.answer: Mijbil is playful, intelligent and full of life. His curiosity is endless: he fumbles with the bathroom tap, turns it on with his paws and soaks himself happily, showing an otter's natural love of water. He is inventive too, making games out of small rubber balls and keeping the whole flat lively with his galloping energy. At first aloof and indifferent, he gradually grows affectionate, following Maxwell about and settling into domestic life with complete trust. He has a wild, restless streak as well; shut in a box for the flight to England, he tears the lining and injures himself, and once aboard he slips out and runs down the aisle, alarming passengers. Strangers in London are equally baffled by him, mistaking him for a seal or even a brontosaurus. Altogether, Mijbil emerges as a mischievous, lovable and unforgettable companion.

boardQuestions.question: Mijbil the Otter beautifully presents the bond between man and animal. Discuss with examples from the chapter.
boardQuestions.answer: The chapter begins with loss: after Jonnie's death, Maxwell's home feels empty, and the friend's suggestion of an otter shows how pets fill emotional gaps. Maxwell's care is evident in every step, from tolerating Mij's water games to making a special box and a difficult travel plan for him. Mij repays this with affection and joy, following the author and turning daily life into play with his tap games and rubber balls. Even strangers share the bond, as the air hostess kindly allows for Mij's comfort and gives him two bowls of water, one to drink and one to play in. The comic guesses in London add gentle humour without any cruelty. The message is clear: animals are sensitive companions that deserve empathy, patience and thoughtful care from human beings.

boardQuestions.question: Read the extract and answer the questions that follow: 'The airline insisted that Mijbil be packed into a box of not more than two feet square. Before the flight, Mij tore the lining of the box and hurt himself. In the aircraft, he slipped out of the box and ran down the aisle, alarming the passengers, until the charming air hostess came to the author's help. She later gave him two bowls of water, one to drink and one to play in.' (a) Why did the airline insist on a box of two feet square? (b) How did Mij behave in the aircraft? (c) What does the air hostess's behaviour tell us about her?
boardQuestions.answer: (a) The airline laid down the rule so that the animal could be carried safely inside the cabin, and Maxwell had to get a suitable box made quickly. (b) Mij behaved restlessly and fearlessly; having already torn the box lining, he slipped out in flight and ran about the plane, frightening passengers until he was caught. (c) The air hostess was kind, patient and fond of animals; she helped the author, kept Mij comfortable and gave him two bowls of water, one for drinking and one for playing, showing rare understanding of a pet's needs.

chapters.title: Madam Rides the Bus
chapters.summary: Valliammai, an eight-year-old called Valli, has no playmates and loves watching the street from her front door. Fascinated by the bus to town, she quietly gathers facts, saves sixty paise and secretly takes the one o'clock bus, insisting she is not a child. A laughing cow makes her journey joyful, but the same cow found dead on the return trip gives her a first taste of sorrow.
hotTopics: Valli's secret plan and careful savings
The one o'clock bus and Valli's refusal to be treated as a child
The jolly conductor and his 'madam' jokes
The running cow and the dead cow: joy and sorrow
Valli's independence and maturity
Theme: a child's curiosity and desire to explore

sections.heading: Plot Summary
points: Valliammai, called Valli for short, is an eight-year-old with no playmates of her own age; her favourite pastime is standing at her front door and watching the street.
The sight of the new bus, full of a fresh set of passengers each hour, fills her with a longing to ride it herself.
She listens carefully to the talk of neighbours and regular bus users, asking a few small, discreet questions to gather facts.
She learns that the town is six miles away, the ride takes forty-five minutes and the fare is thirty paise one way.
Saving every coin, she resists peppermints, toys, balloons and even the merry-go-round at the village fair until she has sixty paise.
One fine spring day she slips out during her mother's afternoon nap, rides to town and back, is shaken by the sight of the cow lying dead on the road, and slips home unnoticed.

keyTerms.meaning: the pet form of Valliammai, the story's eight-year-old heroine
the money paid for a journey on a bus
the bus official who checks tickets and helps passengers
a fairground ride that goes round and round
careful and secret, avoiding attention

sections.trick: Numbers first: 8 years old, 6 miles, 45 minutes, 30 paise fare, 60 paise saved, 1 o'clock bus.
sections.examPointer: This chapter is fact-heavy; examiners love the numbers, so revise them the night before the exam.

sections.heading: Themes and Message
points: Curiosity and the desire to explore the unknown world beyond the village drive the whole story.
Careful planning and self-reliance let a small child achieve her dream without any adult's help.
Innocence meets experience: the playful cow brings laughter, while the dead cow brings the first knowledge of death.
Self-respect matters to Valli, who insists on paying her fare and refuses to be called a child.
The closing talk suggests that the world holds countless experiences, and no one can know them all.
Message: growing up means accepting both the joys and the pains that experience brings.

keyTerms.meaning: a strong desire to know or learn something
depending on oneself without help from others
the quality of being pure, simple and without worldly experience
knowledge gained by actually seeing or doing things
the quality of thinking and acting like a grown-up

sections.trick: Theme in one line: Dream, Discipline, Discovery, Disillusion; the plan, the savings, the ride, the dead cow.
sections.examPointer: Link the theme to the contrast between the two cow sightings; that contrast is the heart of the chapter.

sections.heading: Character Sketch
points: Valli is observant and curious, gathering every detail about the bus through patient watching and listening.
She is determined and disciplined, saving money quietly and resisting every temptation for months.
She is confident and self-respecting, refusing help with the words 'I can get on by myself' and insisting she is not a child.
She is sharp in judgement too, disliking the elderly fellow passenger's ugly earrings and betel-stained lips.
She is sensitive: she laughs at the galloping cow but is deeply shaken when she sees it lying dead.
The conductor is jolly and friendly; he calls Valli 'madam', jokes with the passengers and treats her stubbornness with good humour.

keyTerms.meaning: quick to notice and note things around
firmly resolved to achieve a goal
proud and showing scornful superiority
cheerful and full of good humour
easily affected by feelings and experiences

sections.trick: Valli is a small body with a giant will; the conductor is humour with humanity.
sections.examPointer: For character questions, quote Valli's exact stubborn lines; they carry the marks.

sections.heading: Important Word Meanings
points: Learn each meaning along with the situation in which the word appears.
Use these words to describe Valli's behaviour precisely in long answers.
Match words like haughty and discreet to Valli's actions while revising.
Practise one-line definitions so that you can answer quickly.
Revise this short list frequently before the exam.

keyTerms.meaning: proud and acting superior to others
careful not to attract attention; secret
looked at greedily, as if consuming with the eyes

sections.trick: haughty equals proud, discreet equals careful and secret, devoured equals gazed greedily, jolly equals cheerful.
sections.examPointer: A one-mark meaning question often comes from this list, so learn the exact simple definitions.

sections.heading: Exam Focus
points: Memorise the facts: age eight, distance six miles, ride forty-five minutes, fare thirty paise, savings sixty paise.
Learn Valli's dialogues, especially 'I can get on by myself' and 'I'm not a child'.
Contrast the two cow sightings clearly in any long answer.
Understand the irony of the ending, where adults talk of unknowable things while Valli keeps her secret.
Practise extract-based questions taken from the bus conversations.

keyTerms.meaning: based on a quoted portion of the text
a situation whose real meaning is opposite to what is said
a conclusion reached from evidence in the text
a defining quality of a person in the story
the charge for a passenger's journey

sections.trick: C-O-W for long answers: Curiosity (the plan), On board (the ride), Woe (the dead cow).
sections.examPointer: Answers without specific numbers and dialogues look vague; sprinkle facts to lift your score.

mcqs.question: Who is the author of 'Madam Rides the Bus'?
mcqs.explanation: Vallikkannan, a Tamil writer, wrote this sensitive story of a little girl's bus ride.

mcqs.question: What was Valli's favourite pastime?
options: Playing with children of her age
Standing at her front door and watching the street
Helping her mother in the kitchen
mcqs.explanation: Having no playmates of her own age, Valli's greatest pleasure was watching the street outside her door.

mcqs.question: How old was Valliammai?
mcqs.explanation: Valli was only eight, though she behaved like a grown-up on the bus.

mcqs.question: What was the one-way fare from Valli's village to the town?
mcqs.explanation: The fare was thirty paise one way, so Valli saved sixty paise for the trip both ways.

mcqs.question: How did Valli gather information about the bus journey?
options: By listening carefully to neighbours and regular bus users and asking a few discreet questions
By travelling with her aunt first
mcqs.explanation: Valli planned everything secretly, collecting every detail through careful listening and discreet questioning.

mcqs.question: "I can get on by myself. You don't have to help me. I'm not a child." Who says this, and to whom?
mcqs.explanation: Valli says this when the conductor offers to help her board, insisting that she be treated as a grown-up passenger.

mcqs.question: "The most tempting of all was the ride on the merry-go-round at the village fair." What does this line show about Valli's determination?
options: She was careless with her savings
She resisted even her strongest temptation to save every coin for the bus ride
She loved fairs more than the bus
She spent all her money at the fair
mcqs.explanation: Despite the strongest of all temptations, Valli controlled her desire and saved every coin for her journey.

mcqs.question: "She saw the cow lying dead by the roadside, and the dreadful sight haunted her." What was Valli's reaction on the return journey?
options: She laughed as loudly as before
She wept loudly and asked the bus to stop
She was shocked and no longer wanted to look out of the window
She forgot it as soon as she reached home
mcqs.explanation: The cow she had laughed at on the way to town lay dead on her return trip, and the sight crushed her joy.

mcqs.question: Why did Valli carry out her bus journey in complete secrecy?
options: She wanted to surprise her mother later with a gift
She knew that adults would stop her if they knew, so she planned everything alone during her mother's afternoon nap
Her friends had dared her to do it
The conductor had invited her to travel alone
mcqs.explanation: Valli's plan was entirely her own; she used her mother's nap time so that no adult could prevent the adventure.

mcqs.question: What makes the closing scene of the chapter ironic?
options: The conductor reveals Valli's secret to her mother
Valli confesses everything and is scolded
Her mother says there are many things in this world one cannot know, unaware that quiet little Valli has just returned from a secret adventure
mcqs.explanation: The mother's remark about unknowable things is ironic because Valli has just lived an experience no one else knows about.

boardQuestions.question: What was Valli's deepest desire and how did she plan to fulfil it?
boardQuestions.answer: Valli's deepest desire was to ride the bus that ran between her village and the nearest town. She planned secretly like a grown-up: she learnt that the town was six miles away, the ride took forty-five minutes and the fare was thirty paise, and she saved sixty paise for the trip.

boardQuestions.question: How did Valli save money for her first bus journey?
boardQuestions.answer: Valli saved every coin she could, resisting all her small wishes. She gave up peppermints, toys and balloons, and controlled even her strongest temptation, the ride on the merry-go-round at the village fair. Thus she collected the sixty paise needed to pay her fare both ways.

boardQuestions.question: Describe the conductor's behaviour towards Valli during the bus journey.
boardQuestions.answer: The conductor was a jolly, easy-going man who treated Valli with playful humour. He teased her by calling her 'madam', joked with the passengers and accepted her as a full-fledged traveller when she insisted that she had paid her fare like everyone else. Though he found her amusing, he never really troubled her, and his cheerful manner made her first journey pleasant and memorable.

boardQuestions.question: Compare Valli's feelings when she saw the cow on the two journeys.
boardQuestions.answer: On the way to town, Valli saw a young cow galloping wildly right in front of the bus; the sight was so hilarious that she laughed until there were tears in her eyes. On the return journey, she saw the same cow lying dead by the roadside, struck down by some fast-moving vehicle. The joyful memory turned to horror; the dreadful sight haunted her, she lost all interest in the scenery and sat sad and silent for the rest of the ride.

boardQuestions.question: Draw a character sketch of Valliammai, highlighting her curiosity, confidence and sensitivity.
boardQuestions.answer: Valli is an eight-year-old with no playmates, whose curiosity is fed by watching the street and the bus hour after hour. She is a careful planner: she gathers every fact about the bus by listening and discreet questioning, saves sixty paise by resisting all temptations, and times her trip to her mother's afternoon nap. Her confidence is striking; she boards without help, declares 'I'm not a child', pays her fare like any adult and even judges her fellow passengers sharply, disliking the elderly woman's ugly earrings and betel-stained lips. She devours every passing sight with her eyes, enjoying the ride to the full. She is sensitive too: the galloping cow delights her, but the same cow found dead on the way back crushes her spirits. By the end, quietly carrying her secret home, she shows a maturity far beyond her years.

boardQuestions.question: Valli's first bus ride was a journey from joy to sorrow, from innocence to experience. Justify the statement.
boardQuestions.answer: The ride begins in pure joy: Valli glories in being a paid passenger, devours the passing scenery with her eyes and laughs till tears come when the young cow gallops in front of the bus. The world seems full of wonder. Experience, however, intrudes on the return trip when she sees the same cow lying dead by the roadside; the joyful image turns into a dreadful one that haunts her, and she no longer wishes to look out of the window. Thus in one afternoon she encounters both the beauty and the cruelty of life. The closing scene deepens this growth: she keeps her secret while the adults chat about unknowable things, showing that real experience teaches a child what no conversation can. Her laughter and her silence together mark her passage from innocence to experience.

boardQuestions.question: Read the extract and answer the questions that follow: 'Valli said, "I can get on by myself. You don't have to help me. I'm not a child," and she paid her thirty paise like everyone else on the bus.' (a) Who speaks these words, and on what occasion? (b) What do the words reveal about the speaker's character? (c) How does the conductor respond to her attitude?
boardQuestions.answer: (a) Valli, the eight-year-old heroine, speaks these words when the conductor offers to help her board the bus on her first secret journey. (b) They reveal her fierce independence, self-respect and desire to be treated as an adult; she refuses help and insists on paying her own fare like any grown-up passenger. (c) The conductor takes her attitude sportingly; he teases her gently, calls her 'madam' and keeps the journey light with his humour instead of offending her.

chapters.title: The Sermon at Benares
chapters.summary: Gautama Buddha, once Prince Siddhartha, left his royal life at twenty-five after seeing sickness, old age, death and renunciation, and attained enlightenment under a peepal tree. At Benares he preaches his first sermon on death and grief. Kisa Gotami, mad with grief over her dead son, learns through the mustard-seed task that death is common to all and finds peace in acceptance.
hotTopics: Buddha's early life as Prince Siddhartha
The four sights and the search for enlightenment
Kisa Gotami's grief and her search for medicine
The mustard-seed task
The sermon: similes of ripe fruits and clay pots
Theme: death is common to all; peace through acceptance

sections.heading: Plot Summary
points: Gautama Buddha began life as Prince Siddhartha in northern India; at twelve he was sent away to study the Hindu sacred scriptures, and after returning he married a princess and had a son.
At twenty-five he saw a sick man, an aged man, a funeral procession and a monk begging for alms; these sights of suffering moved him deeply.
He left home and wandered for seven years in search of enlightenment, then sat under a peepal tree until, after seven more days, he was enlightened and became the Buddha, the Awakened One.
The tree came to be called the Bodhi Tree, and the Buddha preached his first sermon at Benares, a holy city on the Ganga.
Kisa Gotami, whose only son had died, carried the body from house to house asking for medicine; people called her mad, and a man directed her to the Buddha.
Asked to bring mustard seeds from a house where no one had ever died, she found death in every house and understood that mortality is universal; her grief then turned to acceptance.

keyTerms.meaning: the name of the Buddha during his princely life
awakening to spiritual truth and wisdom
the peepal tree under which the Buddha attained enlightenment; the tree of wisdom
the grieving mother whose only son had died
tiny seeds the Buddha asked Kisa to bring from a death-free house
the holy city on the Ganga where the Buddha preached his first sermon

sections.trick: Buddha's timeline as 12, 4, 10, 25, 7, 7: schooling at twelve, four years of study, ten years of royal life, departure at twenty-five, seven years of wandering, seven days under the tree.
sections.examPointer: Sequence questions come often; learn the order of events rather than isolated facts.

sections.heading: Themes and Message
points: Death and decay are universal; no house and no heart is free from them.
Wisdom is born of suffering; Kisa Gotami learns the truth through her own search rather than through lectures.
Attachment and lamentation deepen pain, while acceptance brings peace of mind.
The Buddha teaches with compassion, using a simple task and everyday images instead of heavy philosophy.
Life is brief and fragile, like ripe fruits that may fall early and clay pots that eventually break.
Message: give up selfish grief, draw out the arrow of lamentation and attain peace.

keyTerms.meaning: the state of being subject to death
loud weeping and expression of grief
willingly receiving what cannot be changed
pity and concern for the suffering of others
freedom from selfish clinging to people and things

sections.trick: Theme in one line: grief shared is truth learned; death spares no one.
sections.examPointer: For theme questions, connect the mustard-seed task with the sermon's similes; examiners reward such textual linkage.

sections.heading: Character Sketch
points: Kisa Gotami is a grieving mother whose love drives her to carry her dead son from door to door in search of a cure.
She is desperate and blind with sorrow at first, unable to accept the finality of death.
She is humble and teachable; she follows the Buddha's strange condition honestly, house after house, till the truth dawns.
Gautama Buddha is a compassionate guide who heals grief with wisdom rather than with consolation.
The Buddha is a practical teacher; his mustard-seed task lets Kisa discover the truth herself.
The Buddha is serene and wise, using homely similes of fruits and pots to make mortality plain to all.

keyTerms.meaning: deep sorrow, especially for the dead
sympathetic concern for others' suffering
spiritual awakening to ultimate truth
the quality of being modest and teachable
calmness and peace of mind

sections.trick: Two seekers, two journeys: Kisa seeks a medicine, the Buddha sought truth; both searches end in the same understanding of death.
sections.examPointer: Character questions on the Buddha should highlight his method of teaching, not merely list his qualities.

sections.heading: Important Word Meanings
points: Learn the sermon words like lamentation and mortals, since extracts quote them directly.
Understand alms and enlightenment, which describe the Buddha's life and quest.
Match each word to its scene in the chapter for better recall.
Practise writing one-line definitions for every word.
Use these terms in long answers on the sermon for precision.

keyTerms.meaning: loud weeping and wailing in grief
human beings who must one day die
money or food given in charity to beggars
awakening to spiritual knowledge and truth
a state of utter misery and emptiness
a serious religious discourse or teaching

sections.trick: lamentation equals loud grief, mortals equals those who die, alms equals charity, enlightenment equals awakening.
sections.examPointer: Extract-based questions often quote the sermon, so knowing lamentation and mortals helps you decode the passage at once.

sections.heading: Exam Focus
points: Learn Buddha's life sequence: schooling at twelve, royal life, the four sights at twenty-five, seven years of wandering, seven days under the tree.
Know the mustard-seed condition exactly: a house where no one had ever died.
Revise the sermon similes: ripe fruits, clay pots, the young and the old, the foolish and the wise.
Remember the closing idea: peace of mind comes to one who draws out the arrow of lamentation and grief.
Practise value-based questions on grief, acceptance and counselling.

keyTerms.meaning: the sick man, the aged man, the funeral procession and the begging monk
the seeds that had to come from a death-free house
the tree of wisdom under which the Buddha was enlightened
calmness free from grief and anxiety
the holy city where the first sermon was preached

sections.trick: Fruits and pots stand for mortality; the arrow stands for grief; two similes and one cure.
sections.examPointer: A five-mark question often asks for the sermon's teaching; always include at least two similes and the arrow image.

mcqs.question: The chapter 'The Sermon at Benares' is adapted from the writings of:
mcqs.explanation: The text of the chapter is taken from the writings of Betty Renshaw.

mcqs.question: What was the Buddha's name during his princely life?
mcqs.explanation: As a prince he was Siddhartha Gautama, and after enlightenment he became the Buddha, the Awakened One.

mcqs.question: Under which tree did the Buddha attain enlightenment?
mcqs.explanation: He meditated under a peepal tree for seven days; the tree was then renamed the Bodhi Tree.

mcqs.question: What did Kisa Gotami ask for as she went from house to house?
options: Medicine that could bring her dead son back to life
mcqs.explanation: Mad with grief, she begged for a cure for her dead child, while people pitied her as one who had lost her senses.

mcqs.question: Which sights, seen at the age of twenty-five, changed Prince Siddhartha's life?
options: A sick man, an aged man, a funeral procession and a monk begging for alms
A lion, a river, a mountain and a temple
A farmer, a soldier, a trader and a priest
A wedding, a festival, a fair and a feast
mcqs.explanation: These four sights of suffering and renunciation made him leave his palace in search of enlightenment.

mcqs.question: What condition did the Buddha attach when Kisa Gotami asked for medicine for her son?
options: That she should bring flowers from every temple
That she should bring a handful of mustard seeds from a house where no one had ever died
That she should light lamps in every home of the city
That she should feed a hundred monks
mcqs.explanation: The deliberately impossible condition was meant to make her discover for herself that death visits every household.

mcqs.question: "The life of mortals in this world is troubled and brief and combined with pain." Which similes from the sermon illustrate this idea?
options: A river flowing into the sea and a candle burning out
A tree in spring and a bird in flight
Ripe fruits in danger of falling early and clay vessels made by the potter that break
A ship in a storm and a bridge collapsing
mcqs.explanation: The sermon compares human life to fruits that may fall before their time and to pots that break at last.

mcqs.question: Where did the Buddha preach his first sermon?
options: At Benares, the holy city on the Ganga
mcqs.explanation: Benares, a sacred city on the Ganga, was the place of the Buddha's first sermon.

mcqs.question: "Not from weeping nor from grieving will anyone obtain peace of mind." According to the sermon, what must a sorrowing person do instead?
options: Weep longer to honour the dead
Draw out the arrow of lamentation, complaint and grief, and thereby win peace of mind
Keep praying for the return of the lost one
mcqs.explanation: The sermon warns that lamentation only deepens pain; peace belongs to one who overcomes grief.

mcqs.question: What does Kisa Gotami realise as she sits at the wayside watching the city lights twinkle and go out?
options: That her neighbours were jealous of her
That mustard seeds were not available in the city
That she should return home and cook the evening meal
That as the lights go out one by one, so death extinguishes every life, and her grief is the grief of all
mcqs.explanation: The dying lights mirror mortality; she sees that death is common to all and gives up her private search for a cure.

boardQuestions.question: Why did Kisa Gotami go from house to house, and how did people respond to her?
boardQuestions.answer: Kisa Gotami's only son had died suddenly, and she could not accept his death. Carrying the cold body with her, she went from house to house asking for a medicine to bring him back to life. The neighbours pitied her but had no such medicine, and some sadly concluded that the poor woman had lost her senses.

boardQuestions.question: What were the four sights that made Prince Siddhartha leave his home?
boardQuestions.answer: At twenty-five, the prince saw a sick man, an aged man, a funeral procession and a monk begging for alms. These sights showed him the reality of suffering, old age and death, and the possibility of peace through renunciation. Shaken deeply, he left his royal life and set out in search of enlightenment.

boardQuestions.question: How did the mustard-seed task help Kisa Gotami overcome her grief?
boardQuestions.answer: The Buddha asked Kisa Gotami to bring a handful of mustard seeds from a house where no one had ever died. She found mustard seeds easily, but not a single house was free from death; someone in every family had been carried away. Sitting at the wayside and watching the city lights twinkle and go out, she realised that death is common to all. Her selfish sorrow dissolved into acceptance, and she found peace.

boardQuestions.question: Describe the early life of Gautama Buddha before he became the Enlightened One.
boardQuestions.answer: Gautama Buddha began life as Prince Siddhartha Gautama in northern India. At twelve he was sent away to study the Hindu sacred scriptures; he then married a princess, had a son and lived for ten years in royal comfort. At twenty-five, the four sights of sickness, old age, death and renunciation drove him from home. He wandered for seven years in search of truth and finally sat under a peepal tree, where after seven days he was enlightened and became the Buddha, the Awakened One.

boardQuestions.question: Summarise the Buddha's sermon at Benares, bringing out the similes used to teach that death is universal.
boardQuestions.answer: Preaching at Benares, the Buddha says that the life of mortals is troubled, brief and combined with pain. As ripe fruits are early in danger of falling, so mortals, once born, are always in danger of death; as clay vessels made by the potter break at last, so does the life of mortals end. The young and the old, the foolish and the wise, all are caught in the power of death, and no family is untouched by it. He then warns that weeping and grieving cannot bring peace of mind; they only make the pain greater and injure the body. The sorrowing person who seeks peace must draw out the arrow of lamentation, complaint and grief. Whoever draws out that arrow and overcomes sorrow attains peace of mind. Thus a mother's private grief becomes a universal lesson on mortality and acceptance.

boardQuestions.question: Grief rightly understood becomes the door to wisdom. Discuss with reference to Kisa Gotami's experience.
boardQuestions.answer: Kisa Gotami begins in blind grief: refusing to accept her son's death, she carries the body from house to house seeking a medicine to revive him, while neighbours call her mad. The Buddha does not console her with words; he gives her the task of bringing mustard seeds from a house where no one has ever died. In her search she finds seeds in every home but death in every home too. Sitting at the wayside, watching the city lights twinkle and go out, she understands that extinction awaits every life and that death is common to all. Her search for a private cure ends in a shared truth, and her sorrow turns into acceptance and peace. The chapter shows that suffering honestly faced ripens into wisdom.

boardQuestions.question: Read the extract and answer the questions that follow: 'The Buddha said, "Bring me a handful of mustard seeds." And when Kisa Gotami asked in hope, he added that the seeds must come from a house where no one had ever died. House after house gave her seeds, but no house was free from death.' (a) What did Kisa Gotami want from the Buddha? (b) Why did the Buddha set the condition of mustard seeds? (c) What truth did Kisa Gotami discover at last?
boardQuestions.answer: (a) Kisa Gotami, desperate to save her dead son, came to the Buddha seeking a medicine that would bring him back to life. (b) The Buddha set the condition knowing it was impossible to fulfil; the task was a gentle method to make her see death's universality for herself instead of merely accepting a sermon. (c) She discovered that in every house someone had been taken by death, that death is common to all, and that weeping cannot bring peace; only by giving up lamentation can one attain peace of mind.

chapters.title: The Proposal
chapters.summary: Anton Chekhov's farce begins when Ivan Lomov, a wealthy and excitable landowner of thirty-five, visits his neighbour Chubukov to ask for his daughter Natalya's hand. Each time he tries to propose, a quarrel erupts, first over Oxen Meadows and then over the dogs Guess and Squeezer. Only after Lomov faints and revives does Chubukov hastily join the couple's hands and bless the marriage.
hotTopics: Lomov's purpose of visit and his ailments
Quarrel over Oxen Meadows
Quarrel over the dogs Guess and Squeezer
Chubukov's endearments and insults
The fainting and the hurried ending
Satire on marriage of convenience

sections.heading: Plot Summary
points: Lomov, a wealthy landowner of thirty-five who suffers from palpitations and sleeplessness, arrives formally dressed at his neighbour Chubukov's house.
He has actually come to propose to Natalya Stepanovna, Chubukov's twenty-five-year-old daughter, whom he considers a good housekeeper, not bad-looking and well educated.
Before he can propose, the talk drifts to land, and Lomov's mention of Oxen Meadows sparks a fierce dispute about ownership with Natalya and Chubukov.
Lomov leaves feeling unwell; when Chubukov reveals the real purpose of the visit, Natalya is shocked and demands that he be brought back at once.
On his return, the proposal is interrupted again, this time by a silly argument over whose dog is better, Lomov's Guess or the Chubukovs' Squeezer.
The quarrel brings on Lomov's palpitations and he collapses; after he revives, Chubukov hurriedly joins their hands and blesses the marriage.

keyTerms.meaning: Ivan Vassilevitch Lomov, the wealthy, nervous neighbour who comes to propose
Chubukov's twenty-five-year-old daughter, the proposed bride
Stepan Stepanovitch Chubukov, Natalya's father and Lomov's neighbour
the small disputed meadowland claimed by both families
Lomov's dog, said to cost a hundred and twenty-five roubles
the Chubukovs' dog, said to be superior and to cost eighty-five roubles

sections.trick: Track the pattern: Proposal, Quarrel, Exit, Recall; the cycle repeats with the Meadows and then the dogs.
sections.examPointer: Sequence and cause questions are common; remember which quarrel came first and what triggered it.

sections.heading: Themes and Message
points: The play satirises marriages of convenience among the landowning class, where land, money and status matter more than love.
Petty pride over worthless things, a few acres of meadow or a pair of dogs, poisons even the happiest occasion.
Hot temper and stubbornness rule the characters; Lomov and Natalya quarrel out of habit, not hatred.
Hypocrisy appears in Chubukov, who is all endearments in greeting and all abuse in argument.
The hurried ending hints that the couple's married life will be as quarrelsome as their courtship.
Message: ego and the habit of arguing destroy relationships; harmony, not victory in quarrels, builds a home.

keyTerms.meaning: the use of humour and ridicule to expose human folly
people of good social position, especially landowners
acting selfishly for one's own advantage
a light, exaggerated comedy full of absurd situations
restoring friendly relations after a quarrel

sections.trick: Theme equals Land, Love, Ludicrous; property first, proposal second, comedy throughout.
sections.examPointer: When asked about satire, cite the value of the Meadows and the dog dispute as proof of pettiness.

sections.heading: Character Sketch
points: Lomov is a wealthy thirty-five-year-old landowner, nervous and excitable, suffering from palpitations, sleeplessness, trembling lips and a twitch in his right eyebrow.
Lomov is practical and unromantic about marriage; he wants a quiet, settled life and picks Natalya for her housekeeping and education.
Lomov is also petty and stubborn, ready to fight over the Meadows and the dogs even in the middle of his proposal.
Natalya, twenty-five, is quarrelsome and possessive; she battles over land before she even knows the purpose of the visit.
Natalya is impulsive and eager once the truth is out, demanding that Lomov be brought back immediately; she is also a good housekeeper, capable in household matters.
Chubukov is warm-tongued but quick-tempered, greeting Lomov with endearments and abusing him minutes later; an opportunist, he pushes the marriage through the moment Lomov revives.

keyTerms.meaning: a person who imagines or exaggerates illness
a rapid, throbbing beating of the heart
easily stirred to strong feeling or anger
fond of arguing and fighting
one who uses every chance for personal gain

sections.trick: All three share hot temper; what differs is the mask: nervous Lomov, proud Natalya, oily Chubukov.
sections.examPointer: The character section for this play must cover all three characters, so keep two traits and one incident ready for each.

sections.heading: Important Word Meanings
points: Learn the play's vocabulary, especially the insults hurled during the quarrels.
Understand the dog term overshot, which appears in the quarrel extracts.
Know the money and land words that fix the disputes in context.
Use the terms in character answers to sound precise.
Revise them together with the quarrel scenes, since words and scenes are tested together.

sections.heading: Exam Focus

mcqs.question: Who is the author of 'The Proposal'?
mcqs.explanation: The Proposal is a celebrated one-act farce by the Russian dramatist Anton Chekhov.

mcqs.question: Why does Lomov visit Chubukov's house?
options: To ask for Natalya's hand in marriage
mcqs.explanation: Lomov arrives with a marriage proposal, though the quarrels nearly bury his purpose.

mcqs.question: How old is Lomov?
mcqs.explanation: Lomov is thirty-five and calls it a critical age at which one must settle down.

mcqs.question: Who is Natalya Stepanovna to Chubukov?
mcqs.explanation: Natalya, twenty-five, is Chubukov's daughter and the proposed bride.

mcqs.question: What triggers the first quarrel between Lomov and Natalya?
mcqs.explanation: Lomov casually mentions the Meadows; Natalya takes it as a claim, and family pride ignites the fight.

mcqs.question: Which complaint does Lomov repeatedly make whenever he gets excited?
options: Palpitations, trembling lips and a twitch in his right eyebrow
mcqs.explanation: Lomov is a nervous hypochondriac whose lips tremble and whose right eyebrow twitches when he is worked up.

mcqs.question: "My lips are trembling and there's a twitch in my right eyebrow." What does this self-description reveal about Lomov?
options: That he is bold and fearless
That he is telling a lie
That he is a nervous hypochondriac who exaggerates his ailments
That he is angry with Natalya
mcqs.explanation: Lomov keeps listing his imaginary complaints, which shows his excitability and weak nerves.

mcqs.question: "She is a good housekeeper, not bad-looking and well educated." Who says this, and about whom?
mcqs.explanation: Lomov lists these practical qualities as his reasons for choosing Natalya in marriage.

mcqs.question: According to Lomov, what is the history of Oxen Meadows?
options: He bought them last year from a merchant
Chubukov won them in a game of cards
The government gave them to both families jointly
His aunt's grandmother let the Chubukov peasants use them free on condition that they made bricks for her, and the Chubukovs later treated them as their own
mcqs.explanation: This old arrangement is Lomov's proof of ownership, though the Meadows are worth little to either side.

mcqs.question: "Oxen Meadows are ours!" What does this heated claim, together with Lomov's flat refusal to yield, tell us about the dispute?
options: The Meadows are a goldmine that both families badly need
Even land of little worth is defended bitterly, because family pride matters more than sense
Natalya plans to gift the Meadows to Lomov
Lomov wants to sell the Meadows to the government
mcqs.explanation: The Meadows are almost worthless, yet both sides fight furiously, exposing the pettiness of the landed gentry.

boardQuestions.question: Why does Lomov want to marry Natalya, according to his own statement?
boardQuestions.answer: Lomov says he has reached the critical age of thirty-five and suffers from palpitations, sleeplessness and an excitable nature. He feels it is time he led a quiet, settled life. He does not speak of love; he chooses Natalya because she is a good housekeeper, not bad-looking and well educated, and would make a suitable wife.

boardQuestions.question: How does Chubukov receive Lomov when he arrives?
boardQuestions.answer: Chubukov welcomes Lomov with excessive warmth, calling him 'my dear fellow', 'my treasure' and other endearments, and presses him to state the purpose of his visit. His gushing politeness, however, hides impatience, and the moment the talk turns to land he becomes as quarrelsome as anyone else in the play.

boardQuestions.question: Describe the quarrel between Lomov and Natalya over Oxen Meadows.
boardQuestions.answer: Lomov innocently mentions Oxen Meadows, and Natalya at once claims them for her family. Lomov explains that his aunt's grandmother had let the Chubukov peasants use the land free on condition they made bricks for her, but the Chubukovs reject the claim. Both sides shout, call each other grabber and intriguer, and the worthless Meadows are defended like a kingdom. Pale and trembling, Lomov finally staggers out of the house.

boardQuestions.question: How does the quarrel over the dogs begin, and what does it reveal about the characters?
boardQuestions.answer: While trying to propose, Lomov mentions that his dog Guess is first-rate, and Natalya proudly answers that their Squeezer is superior. Chubukov joins in, pointing out that Guess is overshot, and the prices are dragged in, Guess having cost a hundred and twenty-five roubles against Squeezer's eighty-five. Neither side yields an inch, and the silly fight shows how stubborn, childish and quarrelsome both families are, so much so that even a marriage proposal cannot proceed in peace.

boardQuestions.question: Draw a character sketch of Ivan Vassilevitch Lomov.
boardQuestions.answer: Lomov is a wealthy, long-established landowner of thirty-five, but his wealth is matched by weak nerves. He is a hypochondriac: he suffers from palpitations, sleeplessness and an excitable temperament, and constantly refers to his trembling lips, the twitch in his right eyebrow and his foot going to sleep. He is practical and unromantic about marriage; he wants a quiet, settled life at a critical age and selects Natalya because she is a good housekeeper, not bad-looking and well educated. Yet the same man is petty and hot-tempered: he fights savagely over the almost worthless Oxen Meadows and over whether his dog Guess is better than Squeezer, forgetting his proposal in the heat of argument. Nervous yet stubborn, unwell yet argumentative, Lomov is a comic mixture of weakness and pride, and Chekhov uses him to mock the quarrelsome rich.

boardQuestions.question: The Proposal is a satire on marriage and the temper of the landowning class. Discuss with examples from the play.
boardQuestions.answer: Chekhov's farce laughs at a world where marriage has little to do with love. Lomov proposes because, at thirty-five, it is time to settle down, and Natalya is valued as a good housekeeper; the moment Chubukov learns of the proposal he is eager to hurry the couple together. Love is buried under property disputes: the couple's first quarrel is over Oxen Meadows, worth about three hundred roubles, and the second over the dogs Guess and Squeezer, though neither animal is even present. Insults like grabber and intriguer fly as freely as the endearments my dear fellow and my treasure, exposing the shallow manners of the gentry. Even the ending is comic: Lomov faints, the family panics, and the marriage is blessed in a hurry while tempers are still hot, promising a quarrelsome married life.

boardQuestions.question: Read the extract and answer the questions that follow: 'LOMOV boasts that his dog Guess is first-rate. NATALYA and CHUBUKOV retort that Guess is overshot and that their Squeezer, though cheaper, is superior. Neither yields, and Lomov, clutching his heart, falls into a chair. The family cries out in alarm that he is dead, until he revives and Chubukov hastily gives his daughter's hand to him.' (a) What defect is pointed out in Guess? (b) What does the dog quarrel reveal about Lomov and Natalya? (c) How does the play end?
boardQuestions.answer: (a) The Chubukovs say Guess is overshot, that is, his jaw is defective, and insist their Squeezer is a superior dog. (b) The quarrel shows that both Lomov and Natalya are stubborn, proud and childish; even in the middle of a marriage proposal they cannot resist arguing over something as trivial as pets, so their married life promises more of the same. (c) The play ends in comedy: Lomov collapses from palpitations, the family believes for a moment that he is dead, he revives, and Chubukov hurriedly joins their hands and blesses the marriage, glad to have settled his daughter at last.
